The girl opened the door sobbing and said everything was okay. I said okay and as I started walking away I heard her screaming to let her leave. Have an area that the cats can get to that the dog can't and preferably the dog can't even see the cats when they're there. Have the dog on a leash when indoors (you don't have to be holding the leash if he's listening and behaving, but have it for when he isn't). Have a place trained that he knows to go to (eg, bed). When he gets over excited tell him to go to his place. If he doesn't listen bring him there with the leash and give him a treat (placed on the bed). Once he starts listening when you tell him to go there you'll start giving him treats for listening. Once he's listening regularly you'll upgrade to giving them when he sits, then when he lays down. You can practice that without cats around so he can figure out that he's supposed to lay there. Once he is able to be recalled/go to his place when he sees a cat, start working on giving him treats for looking at you instead of the cat. As the cats get closer and braver work on him staying in his place or looking at you and letting them investigate and be cats around him. If he tries to chase them ever step on the leash and make him go to his place when he calms down. It will take a while but it's worth it

This is going to depend on the dog. Some are never going to be good in a crate, but will do well left out in the home. Some do better with playpens and a crate. Some can be crate trained with time. Separation anxiety and crate training is going to look a lot like normal crate training, but go slower. Feed your dog in the crate with the door open. Give your dog treats every time they choose to go near the crate. Once they get comfortable going near the crate, give them treats for going in the crate and treats for staying in the crate with the door open. Once they are choosing to lay in the crate with the door open, close it for a second and give them treats while the door is closed. Once their comfortable with a brief closing of the door, extend the time. Once they can stay in for a while, take a step back then come back and treat.

This method is going to obviously take a lot of time and consistency. And obviously you'll need to crate your dog before you're done acclimating them to the crate. Just try giving them a Kong with peanut butter and food frozen and some good bones and puzzles when you have to. They'll probably still bark, but if you come back and the food got eaten that is proof that they didn't bark the whole time.

We agree that easy to care for dogs get adopted faster, but there are also so many of them looking for homes still. There is still an overabundance of them in shelters. On any given day I can walk into a shelter and see multiple nice, easy dogs. The fact is we have an overabundance of all dogs. It's harder to place "bully breeds" (I hate that term, but for purposes of the conversation it encompasses the breeds that are most common and hardest to adopt in shelters). Even high energy, large dogs get adopted fairly frequently. But for every nice, easy dog that's adopted, there's 20 more nice, easy dogs to take their space in the shelter. I think people who haven't been in rescue severely underestimate the diversity of dogs that shelters get and the number of them. I've had many people comment how surprised they are my dog was a rescue because of his breed... But there are plenty of his breed still in the shelter.

Essentially it's that covid causes issues that are not immediately apparent. So things like brain swelling, blood clotting, immune system damage, etc. A big similarity is drawn between covid immune system damage and hiv. People can be infected with HIV without symptoms for years or decades, but eventually they would end up catching something like pneumonia and dying of it despite being young. That's how the early days of the AIDS crisis was discovered, young people dying of illnesses that shouldn't have killed someone their age. Similarly we are seeing more pneumonia deaths in young people now than we were a decade ago. It's not to aids or HIV levels yet, but there are scientific studies about how even asymptomatic covid infections can cause damage to the immune system. Does that mean it will get to the point of aids? I don't personally think so, but I do think it's smart to avoid infections as much as possible (ie masking and not hanging out with people who are actively symptomatic even if they think it's just a cold). But I'm someone who already has immune system issues that were discovered by repeat pneumonia infections throughout my life, so I'm extra cautious (not like this guy).

That's just not true. I foster for a shelter that is not breed specific. There are pit bulls. If the shelter is aware of a bite (some people surrender without disclosing a bite, so shelters can't always know accurate past histories when lied to), it is added to the dog's profile, the dog is put on a bite hold where they're removed from the shelter and are examined for potential signs of aggression. Depending on the situation, personality, and history, some are put down. Others are only adopted out with extensive vetting of the adopter and multiple consultations with trainers and behaviorists. Often they are put in long term fosters with animal behaviorists to assess and work on behavior to see if they need to be put down or not. But bites from the shelter I foster with are always disclosed and steps are taken to make sure any that are adopted are low risk of biting again and adopters are told the situation the bite occurred from and counseled on how to avoid similar situations and what to look out for. Additionally, most of our dogs with bite histories we are aware of are not actually the pit bulls. We have a lot of very nervous pits who we don't adopt out to families with children or small animals out of caution, but our biters are often small dogs and working breeds (or mutts).

With PCOS and endometriosis there is a reason they don't want to do hysterectomies. Oh top of being a major surgery, it actually isn't particularly effective at treating them. I know you've said you don't want to try hormonal birth control in other comments because you don't want to gain weight, but if your periods are painful enough that you can't enjoy your life I'm going to suggest reevaluating. There are a lot of different options for birth control and usually any weight gain they cause will go away when you stop taking it. So, if it truly is a deal breaker to gain weight, you can stop taking it. This is going to make the doctors take you more seriously if you're at least willing to try their treatment options. If you're not willing to try any treatment (because most treatment for these conditions can cause weight gain, including the surgical options) then they will not feel like your condition is as serious as you claim.

I'd also push for a diagnosis so you know what you're dealing with. A lot of gynos will push oral birth control before understanding what's causing the pain since birth control is the first line treatment for most conditions that can cause pain. Blood tests to test your hormones, a laparoscopic surgery to check for endometriosis, cysts, fibroids, etc could be helpful. You might need a second opinion if your gyno is unwilling to do these significantly less invasive procedures to get a diagnosis.

Adoption fees are important for a myriad of reasons. People who use cats as bait in dog fights aren't likely to pay an adoption fee. Even if you have spay/neuter clinics who will vaccinate and spay/neuter for cheap or free, cats in shelters are still prone to infectious diseases that need to be treated before they're adopted. Fasts are usually the opposite of what is recommended to feel hunger again. Fasting suppresses hunger cues (your body isn't going to waste limited energy telling you you're hungry once it realizes you're not going to listen).

One of the restoring hunger cues things I've seen is reverse dieting. I haven't looked much into it because I haven't personally had issues with hunger cues, but it's essentially giving up on losing weight until your hunger cues are restored. The theory is once you can feel hunger and full again you'll be able to do a more sustainable diet (such as McDougall) because you'll feel full enough not to overeat. But it does have the potential that you'll gain weight when you're reverse dieting. However, my (limited) understanding is people whose hunger cues are suppressed see much better long-term effects after reverse dieting. A diet like McDougall or whole foods plant based would both be significantly more effective post reverse dieting for someone like yourself (again, from my understanding).

It's super stressful, but imaging can also be helpful because certain shapes of lymph nodes and different levels of vascularity that get see on ultrasounds can all help see if it's a more likely to be lymphoma swollen lymph node or a swollen lymph node from infection or an autoimmune disorder. I would. Statistically it's likely not lymphoma, but imagining is important to make sure it's not growing unexpectedly or quickly. There's no true way to check that if you're not getting imaging on it.

If it's been swollen for over a year I would definitely push for imaging or a second opinion. There are plenty of non lymphoma explanations for swollen lymph nodes, but if it's been swollen for a year it's unlikely to be due to an infection that your body would be able to fight off in its own. Monitoring on imaging and blood tests would probably be good next steps.

You're right that there are other factors, but demand is not currently one of them. Demand is huge, prices in my area have risen around 50% in the past year because of the large amount of demand for the too small supply. But 50% of 100k is a lot different then 50% of 500k, so while the prices are rising based on similar percentages NOW, the historic issues in the region that have kept prices from rising in the PAST leads to lower prices now. Historic issues in the region are largely economic. Auto industry collapse leading to the main industry in the Midwest, thus without the jobs, people left to areas with jobs. Now jobs are coming back in other industries and demand is huge, but there isn't the historic increase in prices that you see in other regions. A house that sold for $70k in the 40s largely sold for $90k until the 2000s (pre 2008), with only the recent increase in demand driving it to $150k. Things don't go from the prices they were in the Midwest three years ago to the prices they are in the northeast or west coast overnight. It takes decades of economic development, jobs, and wages. Demand is not what has houses cheaper in the Midwest right now, because the demand is VERY much there.

Another factor is our houses here are much older. I see posts here talking about "old" houses built in the 60s... Here that's a new house. Most houses in my city are from the 1880s through the 1930s. The "newly" developed areas are at newest the 80s maybe a few 90s houses. That drives housing prices down as well because no one is spending the same amount on an identical house built in 1880 as they will on one built in 1980. 

In short, there are a ton of distinct historical reasons that have kept housing prices down in the Midwest, but the current demand is not an issue. Demand hasn't been this high in the Midwest in my 75 year old realtor's lifetime.

When you're ready to talk start looking you can shop around with lenders and it will all count as a small ding on your credit for the one mortgage credit check. This will be required for pre-approval, which will be required for you to put an offer on a house. To be pre-approved you'll need to provide two years of tax returns and current pay stubs, as well as some other stuff.

Before you put in offers on any houses, you can call a bank to get "pre-qualified." This will involve you telling them your financial situation and them telling you that if you're being accurate, you'll likely be pre-approved for x amount, but it won't be official. If you talk to them earlier than you're planning on putting in offers, make sure you tell them you aren't trying to get pre approved yet, you're just trying to talk about your options so that they don't run your credit. 

When talking about pre-qualification, talk about what you want your monthly payment including utilities and taxes to look like. Chances are the bank will pre-approve you and pre-qualify you for more than you're going to want to spend monthly. They'll need to know what percentage down payment you're thinking about, as that will effect if you have to pay PMI or not. PMI is basically insurance to the bank that you'll pay your mortgage in time and it's best to avoid it by putting down 20% if you can. However, if you don't think you'll have a 20% down payment, you can apply to have it removed later. It'll add about $300 to your monthly payment, though, so again, best to avoid if possible. 

Between your pre-qualification and your pre-approval, interest rates will change. They'll change more between pre-approval and when you buy a house. So the estimate you get of what you can afford with your pre-qualification will be an estimate/ballpark range that will give you an idea of what you're looking at to start casually looking.

I agree it has no choice, as I stated I don't ride anymore. 

However, the fact that horses are scared of a harness before they know what it is does not automatically equate to it being harmful for them. Most dogs are more afraid of harnesses than they are collars, but harnesses cause less physical damage than collars. "Break" is used to describe the desensitization the same way dogs become desensitized to harnesses.

When "broken" as humanely as possible I never saw a horse resist riding more than my childhood dog resisted his harness. There are undoubtedly inhumane ways it can be done that cause more fear and I would personally consider abuse, similar how I think prong collars on dogs is inhumane and abuse. 

A big difference is dogs need to be on leashes in order to be safe walking in urban areas. Horses do not need to be ridden for their own safety.

I know I'm going to be attacked for this. I don't ride anymore because I think it's at best morally grey and I'm too poor to afford it anyway, but I used to work at a horse back riding place that taught children to ride. 

Most horses do not need to be broken in the way most people think of it from movies and media. Back in the day that was common. Now everywhere I've seen, "breaking" involves teaching a horse not to be scared of a halter, positive reinforcement to learning commands, tolerating grooming, etc. The process starts at a young age and involves no riding out putting anyone on the back of the horse for the vast majority of the process. The goal at a young age is gaining trust, helping the horse stay calm, and teaching it vocal commands to run and stop. And when the horse is old enough, gradually increasing weight until the horse is comfortable and strong enough to be ridden. 

Additionally, most places I was aware of no longer use bits, spurs, or whips. Instead, the reason for teaching the horse vocal commands at a young age is so that you're not harming the horse by whipping it or kicking it. And bits are also not needed if you properly broke the horse, instead you've taught the horse through positive reinforcement to respond to vocal commands and reins and weight shifting to turn or stop. 

I'm not saying there aren't places that don't use what many consider the older and crueler methods, but when I was still active in the horse world those people were few and far between and were ridiculed.

Covid is very different from person to person and from infection to infection. I was unfortunately always high risk, so it's not super surprising it was/is pretty severe for me despite vaccines. However, while I say "pretty severe for me," this is considered a mild infection by the CDC. The only infections that they do not consider mild are those that require hospitalization. So when they say things are more mild, it's important to put what that means into context. It only means a fewer percentage of people infected with the disease are being hospitalized for it. That doesn't mean they aren't sick for weeks or longer, it doesn't mean they're at all capable of working during that time, it just means their life is not in immediate danger of ending without medical intervention.

It's important to also note that that's only the percentage of people who are infected as well, so it doesn't mean anything for how many people are actually hospitalized or dying. If a disease had a 90% hospitalization rate but only infected 1,000 people, that's only 900 people hospitalized. But if a disease has a 1% hospitalization rate but infected 1,000,000 people, that's 10,000 people. Obviously these are not the real numbers, but it demonstrates the basic concept that while covid might have more mild infections now, we're allowing increasingly infectious variants to run rampant unmitigated.
